The other 78% are about everything else, so this is not only about AI. Click: and what do they ask most? Those questions are now the agent's prompt templates: 15 on its start page, five per section. Then controlling AI spending: 17% of the AI requests need help with cost or proving value. And comparing Azure prices, the FinOps core; in my latest audit of real chats, pricing their own setup was what people typed most. One fundamental before we look at the portals: how Microsoft prices AI. It is usage-based: you pay for the work AI does, not a flat fee per user. And the unit is simple: one AI credit is one US cent. Click: Copilot Credits are Microsoft's one currency for usage-based AI: Copilot Studio agents, Copilot Cowork and Work IQ. At pay as you go, one credit is one cent. A Copilot Studio agent's generative answer is 2 credits, 2 cents; an agent action 5; grounding in your tenant's data 10, so a complex grounded answer is about 12 cents. Employee-facing agents used by someone with a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence are included, within fair use. You pay as you go through an Azure subscription, where it shows as Microsoft Copilot Studio, prepay in packs of 25,000 credits a month, or commit for a year at a discount. Click: GitHub uses the same unit: GitHub AI Credits, and one AI credit is one cent. Copilot Business includes 1,900 credits a user a month and Enterprise 3,900, pooled across the organization; beyond that, usage is billed per credit within the budgets you set in dollars. Code completions stay unlimited. Underneath, every chat or agent run is tokens, priced by model and converted to credits. Click: your own AI apps in Microsoft Foundry are billed per token, input, output and cached, priced by model and deployment type, mostly per million tokens; provisioned throughput is billed per hour. That shows up in dollars on the Azure bill. So the same AI work is counted in credits in some places and in dollars and tokens in others. That is the next slide. Sources: Microsoft Learn, "Usage-based billing: what you see in the Microsoft 365 admin center vs. your Azure bill", "Billing rates and management" for Copilot Studio, "Meters for Microsoft Copilot pay-as-you-go services" and "Billing concepts for Microsoft Foundry"; GitHub Docs, "Usage-based billing for organizations and enterprises".

Starting with AI means governing your agents, so a quick quiz. Click: Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for AI agents: one registry to see, govern and secure every agent, whoever built it. It lists Copilot Studio agents, published Foundry agents, and agents on Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI once you connect those platforms. Click: the Responses API, the newer API and the one Microsoft recommends for new apps. It's stateful: pass previous_response_id and it carries the conversation for you. And it has built-in tools: web search, file search, code interpreter and MCP servers. Click: Chat Completions, the classic. Stateless: you send the whole conversation with every call. Still supported, and it works with almost every model and SDK. One catch for agents: on the newest reasoning models, a Chat Completions call with function tools fails unless you turn reasoning off, so Microsoft Learn points you to the Responses API for tool calling. Click: my app uses these APIs with tools and memory: it plans, calls tools and remembers. What does Agent 365 show? Hands up, or type in the chat, if it shows up in the registry. Click: Nothing. Until you register it, Agent 365 doesn't see an agent: it's a model endpoint, tokens in and tokens out, running as your app's key or managed identity, with no agent identity. Microsoft Learn even calls this an ephemeral agent: there is no agent to create, update or delete. In Foundry its cost lands in the Non-agent requests row from the screenshot. Click: register it, and then it's an agent. It gets its own Microsoft Entra agent identity and a place in the Agent 365 registry, with an owner. Conditional Access and identity protection apply, which need Entra Agent ID licensing; Defender and Purview see the same agent; and in Foundry it gets its own cost row, with its traces linked. Three ways: built in Foundry, publish it and it appears in the registry automatically, and Copilot Studio agents are there the moment you create them. Your own code: the Agent 365 CLI, a365 setup all, registers a blueprint and an agent identity, and the Agent 365 SDK adds notifications, Work IQ tools and observability through Microsoft OpenTelemetry. Bedrock or Vertex AI: connect the platform and its agents sync, with no development work. One gotcha: creating a Microsoft Entra identity alone doesn't register the agent instance. Honest footnote: my own FinOps agent is one of these today. If someone pushes back: a published Foundry agent called with agent_reference does run as that agent, and Defender's discovery of local agents covers managed devices, not a server calling a model. Sources, all on Microsoft Learn: the Agent 365 overview and registry, agent identities in Microsoft Entra Agent ID, publishing agents in Microsoft Foundry, and the Responses API.

How it's built. Click: you, signed in with your own Microsoft Entra account; every read uses your own rights. Click: one agent serves every chat: a .NET 10 app on Azure App Service, built on Microsoft Agent Framework. Click: it thinks with a model in your own Microsoft Foundry account, today gpt-6.1-terra, through the Responses API, called with a managed identity, so there is no key in the app. Click: between the agent and your data sit thin tools, and the rules live in code, not in the prompt: tokens, a query sandbox, a throttle queue and safety. The next slide is why each one was needed. Click: then the data: Azure Resource Manager for cost, Resource Graph, Advisor and Azure Monitor; Microsoft Graph for licences and users; Log Analytics; Azure Storage for cost exports; the public Retail Prices API; and Microsoft Learn through its MCP server. The model writes each API call itself; the host routes, checks and crops it. Click: and new this week, the Microsoft 365 Copilot cost management API, in preview on Microsoft Graph beta: Copilot Credits per user, group and service, balances, spending policies, alerts and credit requests. The agent uses all 23 read operations, and the 9 change operations only after you approve the exact request. It has its own admin-consent tokens, one for reading and one for changes, and because it reports credits, not money, the agent prices them at the 1-cent pay-as-you-go meter. Around it: a Vue 3 front end that streams the answer as it is written, OpenTelemetry into Application Insights, and azd up deploys it all into the customer's own subscription with Bicep. And it's built with GitHub Copilot: over 700 commits since 15 March, over 300 of them co-authored with Copilot, and 13 repo skills that deploy, release, evaluate sessions and investigate logs.

Why it was hard. And how I solved it.

The problem How I solved it
API scopesEntra issues one token per resource: Azure, Graph, Log Analytics and Storage each need their own.7 consent tiers, 6 tokens per user, each sent only to its own host.
Big data, one stepOne API response can hold thousands of rows, and every extra model round adds seconds.The model writes the calls and a C# query; a sandbox returns only the result. Up to 50 calls in one step.
ThrottlingCost Management allows 12 query units per 10 seconds per tenant. Copilot’s cost API throttled at about the tenth report in a row.One cost query at a time per tenant. Wait what the service says, else exponential backoff: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 s.
Never guess, never deleteA model can fill a gap with a guess, or be talked into a change.A failed read is unknown, never zero. DELETE is blocked in code; every change waits for your click.
Copilot cost API, in previewNew at Ignite 2026. Credits only, no currency, and the admin center’s views use an internal API no app can call.Its own read and change consent. The admin center’s three views rebuilt from Graph beta, credits priced at 1 cent.

Each piece is simple. All of them in one answer, fast and safe: that was the hard part.

What made it hard was not one big thing but five at once. Click: API scopes. Microsoft Entra gives a token for one resource at a time, so Azure Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Log Analytics and Storage each need their own token and their own consent. And adding admin-only scopes to a shared token would have broken it for every user who hadn't consented to them. So: 7 consent tiers, 6 tokens per user, each sent only to its own host. Tokens stay in memory; only an encrypted refresh token is stored. The Copilot cost write scopes are a tier of their own, which "connect all" never asks for. Click: big data in one step. A cost or inventory response can run to thousands of rows, far more than the model should read, and every extra round to the model adds seconds. So the model writes the call plus a C# LINQ query, and the host runs it in a sandbox: up to 16,000 characters, 20 million steps and 10 seconds, with at most 48 KB back. Up to 50 URLs go in one call, 4 at a time, with one query across all of them. In October, rounds spent only re-typing numbers to do arithmetic were 17% of model time; now that happens inside the call. Click: throttling. Cost Management allows 12 query units per 10 seconds, 60 per minute and 600 per hour per tenant, one unit per month of data, plus limits per subscription and per client type. So the host runs one cost query at a time per tenant, waits exactly what the service names, up to 5 attempts and 5 minutes of waiting, and shows the user that it is waiting. Where no wait is named, it backs off exponentially with jitter: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 seconds. One discovery: without a ClientType header, requests share a default quota; on 18 November that quota answered 429 with 0 left, while the same queries naming their client had 1,995 left. The Copilot cost API throttles by request rate: about the tenth report in a row drew a 429 with a 30-second wait, so those calls go one at a time and completed reports are cached for 15 minutes. Click: never guess, never delete. A failed, denied or throttled read is reported as unknown, never as zero. DELETE is blocked centrally, POST is allow-listed, and every change shows the exact request and waits for the user's click. Click: and the newest one, the Microsoft 365 Copilot cost management API, announced at Ignite and in preview on Microsoft Graph beta. It reports Copilot Credits only, no currency, and the admin center's own Consumption views read an internal portal API that no app registration can call. So the agent has its own admin-consent tiers for reading and for changes, builds the admin center's three views, Policies, Users and groups, and Services and agents, from Graph with their exact columns, and prices credits not billed yet at the 1-cent pay-as-you-go meter. Click: each of these is simple on its own; doing all of them inside one chat answer, fast and safely, is what made it hard. One more: every model call carries about 27,000 tokens of instructions and tool definitions, so each turn gets only the tools it can use, and past 100,000 tokens a chat continues from a recap, because long chats waited 10 to 17 seconds for the first word. Sources: Microsoft Learn, "Manage Azure costs with automation", for the QPU quotas; the repository's HttpHelper, CostQueryCoordinator and JsonQuery code for the rest.

  3. 3Gated deployOne failure stops it, with no re-run

What fails becomes a new test, fixed at its cause.

How do I keep it right? Click: every push to main runs 914 C# tests, 226 Node tests and 98 desktop and mobile browser tests. Click: then the live gate: 23 real questions, each on the real model with real Azure tools, and a second model judges every answer: accepted, grounded, complete and efficient. Click: the gate: one failure stops the deploy, with no re-run. Click: after the release, 15 more questions run as a quality report that never blocks, and every few weeks I score real conversations, read-only and pseudonymised. Click: what fails becomes a new test, fixed at its cause: never by re-running, switching models or loosening the rubric. A real example from Thursday: five evals failed in five different places after I made answers shorter, and each time a correct fact had been reworded wrongly. The fix was one principle in the prompt: shorten by leaving things out, never by rewording what stays. Click: and this is the real run that deployed what's in production now, on GitHub: the regression tests took 6 minutes 17 and the 23 live questions 12 minutes 51, side by side, then build and deploy 2 minutes 43. 15 minutes 45 seconds from push to production, and the gate's verdict: 100% green, 23 passed, 0 failed.

Every answer is judged.

  1. AcceptedIt answers what was asked
  2. GroundedEvery figure from a real call
  3. CompleteNothing asked for is missing
  4. EfficientNo wasted calls or rounds

A different model judges. Code checks have the last word.

How is an answer judged? Each of the 23 questions runs through the real chat handler, on the real model with real Azure tools. Then a second, different model judges it, seeing the question, every tool call with its arguments and results, and the full timeline. Click: accepted: does it answer what was asked? Click: grounded: does every figure come from a call it really made? Click: complete: is nothing that was asked for missing? Click: efficient: the judge counts avoidable calls, rounds and seconds, and code turns those counts into a score from 1 to 5; at least 3 to pass. Click: this is the gate's report for the version in production: 23 passed, 0 failed, a median of 19.1 seconds per answer, 73 tool calls, efficiency 4.9 out of 5. The published report withholds the answers: only the questions, tool outcomes, timings and verdicts are public. Click: the judge never has the last word. Code checks required and forbidden tools, tool failures and time budgets, and a positive verdict can't override a failed call. The agent runs on gpt-6.1-terra and the judge on gpt-6.1-sol, so no model grades itself. The theory: Zheng et al., "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge", NeurIPS 2023: strong LLM judges agree with human preferences over 80% of the time, as often as humans agree with each other. They also favour answers by position, length and their own style, which is why a different model judges and code checks override it.
